You talk about the past with the compound perfect: am mers, am văzut, am fost, am avut.
On Saturday we went to the Turda Gorge.
To form the compound perfect: the auxiliary “a avea” (am, ai, a, am, ați, au) + past participle.
To form the past participle: -at, -ut, -it, -ât and the irregular forms (făcut, mers, văzut, fost).
To use the compound perfect with reflexive verbs: m-am trezit, s-a întâmplat.
To make the past negative: n-am mers, nu ai văzut.
To use time expressions: ieri, aseară, săptămâna trecută, acum doi ani, deja, încă nu.
On Monday, Mr Rusu comes to Nora’s desk with a coffee in his hand. He saw some photos from the Turda Gorge on Ana’s phone and wants to hear the whole story.
Good morning! I heard you went to the Turda Gorge. How was it?
Good morning! It was wonderful. We left on Saturday at eight and got there at nine.
Well, not all of us at eight. Radu was an hour late. He woke up at half past eight!
Typical of musicians! And what did you do there?
We climbed the main trail, crossed the wooden bridge and saw the cliffs. We took hundreds of photos.
Did you see the vultures too? Rare vultures live there.
Yes! We saw two. But I didn’t manage to photograph them, they flew away too fast.
And the weather? I know there was a strong wind on Saturday afternoon.
Exactly. At lunchtime it was warm, but at four the wind started blowing and it turned cold. Thank goodness for Mrs Pop’s hat!
Radu didn’t have a hat. So Nora gave him her red scarf. The new one!
Ana! It was nothing special. He was just cold.
Well, I’m glad you had fun. Now, unfortunately, we have to work. Have you already read the report on the Wolphard House?
Not yet. I’ll read it now!
“ați fost / a fost” = past of “a fi” (you were / it was)
“s-a trezit” = past of “a se trezi” (he woke up)
“ați făcut / am făcut” = past of “a face” (you did / we did)
“am văzut / ați văzut” = past of “a vedea” (we saw / you saw)
“să bată” = the form of “a bate” after “să”
“nu a avut” = past of “a avea” (he didn’t have)
“i-a dat” = past of “a da” (she gave him)
The auxiliary is joined to the participle: “am mers” sounds almost like “ammers”. The stress falls on the participle: am MERS, am VĂ-zut.
In speech “nu am” becomes “n-am”, “nu ai” → “n-ai”, “nu a” → “n-a”. They are pronounced as one syllable.
With reflexive verbs, the pronoun is attached to the auxiliary: “m-am trezit”, “s-a întâmplat”, “v-ați distrat”.
The participle endings are pronounced clearly, with a final “t”: “văzut”, “găsit”, “urcat”. Don’t swallow the “t”!
The compound perfect is the past tense used most often in Romanian, especially in speech. It is formed with the auxiliary verb “a avea” (in its short form) + the past participle of the verb.
The participle does NOT change with person or gender: “eu am lucrat”, “ea a lucrat”, “ei au lucrat”. Very good news: all verbs, even “a fi”, use the same auxiliary “a avea”.
Careful: in the 3rd person singular the auxiliary is “a”: “el a mers”, not “el are mers”.

“Nu” goes before the auxiliary. In speech “nu am” often becomes “n-am”.
Questions are made with intonation, as in the present:
What did you do on Saturday?
Where did you go on holiday?
Only a few short words can come between the auxiliary and the participle: “mai”, “și”, “tot”, “cam”: “Am mai fost acolo.” (I’ve been there before.)
With reflexive verbs, the reflexive pronoun goes before the auxiliary and is joined to it with a hyphen.
Direct and dative pronouns behave the same way: “L-am văzut” (I saw him), “Am văzut-o” (I saw her – “o” goes AFTER the participle!), “I-am dat fularul” (I gave him the scarf).
“Acum” + a period means “ago”: “acum doi ani” = “two years ago”. Watch the order: “acum” comes FIRST.

On Saturday evening Nora came home very late, at ten. I waited for her by the door all evening, like a dog. I’m not proud of it.
She came in tired, with her boots covered in mud and her cheeks red from the wind. But she smiled the whole time. Mrs Pop noticed at once.
“Well? How was it?” she asked. “Did you wear the hat?”
“I wore it,” answered Nora. “You were right. At four it got terribly cold. Without your hat, we would have frozen.”
“And Radu? I know he didn’t take a hat. He never does.”
Nora was silent for a second. Then she said: “I gave him my scarf.”
Mrs Pop said nothing. But she put the water on for tea and quietly sang an old song. I understood: it’s a song she only sings when she is very happy.
On Sunday it rained all day, exactly as forecast. Nobody went out. Nora slept until eleven. Then she sat on the red rug and looked at the photos on her computer.
I saw the photos too, because I sat on the keyboard. I saw high cliffs, a green river, a wooden bridge and blue sky. And I saw lots of photos of Radu.
Radu on the bridge. Radu by the river. Radu with the red scarf round his neck, laughing. Radu playing the violin on a rock, with the mountains behind him.
“He took his violin to the mountains?” asked Mrs Pop, who came in with the tea.
“Yes. He played Enescu in the canyon. The echo was incredible. Some German tourists applauded.”
Mrs Pop looked at the photo for a long time. Then she said quietly: “His grandfather once played at the Turda Gorge too. Fifty years ago. For me.”
Nora looked up. “Mr Vasile played the violin?”
“Not the violin. The fluier, the shepherd’s flute. But it was the most beautiful concert of my life.”
Then Mrs Pop left the room. Nora stayed looking at the photo. I fell asleep on the keyboard and, without meaning to, typed a whole page of “jjjjjjjj”.
